title: Sleep In
brief: Tells you whether someone gets to sleep in.
description: You get to sleep in on any day that isn't a weekday, and also on vacation days no matter what. Given whether it's a weekday and whether it's vacation, figure out if sleeping in is allowed.
solution:
def sleep_in(weekday, vacation):
    return (not weekday) or vacation
hints: Think about when sleeping in is NOT allowed, then flip it.
You can combine 'not weekday' with 'or vacation' in one return line.
explainer: Sleeping in fails only when it's a weekday and not vacation, so the opposite of that condition covers every other case.

title: Monkey Trouble
brief: Checks if two monkeys are both smiling or both not smiling.
description: Two monkeys get into trouble together only when they match: either both are smiling or neither one is. Given each monkey's smile status, decide if there's trouble.
solution:
def monkey_trouble(a_smile, b_smile):
    return a_smile == b_smile
hints: There's no need for if/else here.
Compare the two booleans directly with ==.
explainer: Two booleans are equal exactly when they match, which is exactly the trouble condition described.

title: Sum Double
brief: Adds two numbers, but doubles the result if they're equal.
description: Normally you just add the two numbers together. But if the two numbers happen to be the same, return double their sum instead.
hints: Start by computing a + b, then check if a equals b.
Doubling the sum when a == b is the same as multiplying by 2.
explainer: When a equals b the sum is doubled with * 2; otherwise the plain sum is returned unchanged.

title: Diff 21
brief: Finds how far a number is from 21, with a penalty for going over.
description: Return how far the number n is from 21. If n is 21 or under, just return the plain difference. If n is over 21, return double the amount it went over by.
hints: Split this into two cases with an if/else on n <= 21.
For the 'over 21' case, compute n - 21 first, then double it.
explainer: For n <= 21 the plain gap 21 - n is returned; for n > 21 the overshoot n - 21 is doubled as a penalty.

title: Parrot Trouble
brief: Decides if a talking parrot is causing trouble based on the time.
description: A parrot causes trouble if it's talking and the hour is either before 7 (too early) or 20 or later (too late). Given whether it's talking and the current hour (0-23), figure out if there's trouble.
solution:
def parrot_trouble(talking, hour):
    return talking and (hour < 7 or hour >= 20)
hints: There are two conditions on hour to combine with 'or' first.
The parrot only matters if talking is True, so 'and' that whole hour check.
explainer: The hour check covers 'too early' and 'too late', and the result only counts when talking is also True.

title: Makes 10
brief: Checks if either number is 10, or if they add up to 10.
description: Given two whole numbers, return True if either one of them is 10, or if adding them together makes 10.
solution:
def makes10(a, b):
    return a == 10 or b == 10 or a + b == 10
hints: You need to check three separate conditions, joined with 'or'.
Don't forget the case where neither number is 10 by itself, but together they add to 10.
explainer: Any one of the three 'or' conditions being true is enough to make the whole expression True.

title: Near Hundred
brief: Checks if a number is close to 100 or close to 200.
description: A number counts as 'near' 100 or 200 if it's within 10 in either direction. Given a number, return True if it lands close to either landmark.
solution:
def near_hundred(n):
    return abs(100 - n) <= 10 or abs(200 - n) <= 10
hints: The built-in abs() function gives you distance without worrying about sign.
Check distance from 100 and distance from 200, joined with 'or'.
explainer: abs(100 - n) measures the gap to 100 and abs(200 - n) measures the gap to 200; being within 10 of either one satisfies the 'or'.

title: Pos Neg
brief: Checks if two numbers have opposite signs, or both negative if asked.
description: Given two numbers and a negative flag, normally return True when one number is positive and the other is negative. But if the negative flag is True, only return True when both numbers are negative.
hints: Handle the 'negative' flag as its own branch first.
Zero is neither positive nor negative, so it should never satisfy either branch.
explainer: When negative is True the function demands both numbers be strictly below zero; otherwise it checks that exactly one side is negative and the other positive.

title: Not String
brief: Adds 'not ' to the front of a string, unless it's already there.
description: Given a string, return a new string that starts with 'not '. If the string already starts with 'not ', just return it unchanged.
hints: The .startswith() method checks a prefix for you.
Only add the prefix in the case where startswith('not ') is False.
explainer: startswith('not ') detects the exact 4-character prefix including the space, so 'not' alone (no trailing space) still gets the prefix added.

title: Missing Char
brief: Removes the character at a given position from a string.
description: Given a string and an index n, return the string with the character at position n taken out.
solution:
def missing_char(str, n):
    return str[:n] + str[n + 1:]
hints: Slice the string into the part before n and the part after n.
str[n+1:] skips over the character you want removed.
explainer: str[:n] keeps everything before index n and str[n+1:] keeps everything after it, so the character exactly at n is dropped.

title: Front Back
brief: Swaps the first and last characters of a string.
description: Given a string, swap its first and last characters and return the result. An empty string or a single character should come back unchanged.
hints: Handle the length-0-or-1 case separately so you don't slice weirdly.
The middle part, str[1:-1], stays exactly where it is.
explainer: Only the first and last letters trade places; str[1:-1] grabs everything in between and keeps its order.

title: Front 3
brief: Repeats the first 3 characters of a string 3 times.
description: Take the first 3 characters of a string (or the whole string if it's shorter than 3) and repeat that chunk 3 times.
hints: Python slicing never errors even if the string is shorter than 3.
Multiplying a string by 3 repeats it 3 times.
explainer: str[:3] safely grabs up to 3 characters no matter the string's length, and * 3 repeats that chunk.

title: Back Around
brief: Moves the last character of a string to the front.
description: Given a non-empty string, take its last character and move it to the very front, shifting everything else over by one.
hints: str[-1] grabs just the last character.
str[:-1] grabs everything except that last character.
explainer: The last character is pulled out with str[-1] and placed in front of the remaining str[:-1] slice.

title: Or 35
brief: Checks whether a number divides evenly by 3 or by 5.
description: Given a number, return True if it's evenly divisible by 3 or by 5 (or both).
solution:
def or35(n):
    return n % 3 == 0 or n % 5 == 0
hints: The % operator gives you the remainder after division.
A remainder of 0 means it divides evenly.
explainer: n % 3 == 0 catches multiples of 3 and n % 5 == 0 catches multiples of 5; the 'or' covers both.
